provenance.method: gap = |goal - baseline| directionally; recovered = |after - baseline| directionally; remaining = gap - recovered; goal_met = remaining <= 0 (PLAN §4.1 Improve-loop gap arithmetic, rubric R-IMP-04, BoK IV.C.1)

artifact.notes: No claim upgraded in transit: the mean promise is kept (goal met, remaining -0.78), the every-ticket promise honestly is not.

panels.narrative: Routine tickets averaged 26.71 business hours against the 8-hour service-catalog promise (baseline n=127); Q2 status-chase and rework costs ran near $7,742/quarter.
Baseline: stable (zero rule-1/rule-4 signals) yet one-sided Cpk -0.96 -- the process was built to miss the promise every time, not having a bad week.
Cut mean resolution time to 8.0 business hours by 2026-10-31 without degrading the reopen-rate or overtime guardrails.

The once-a-day triage batch (53.5% of delay tallies) and the late manager-approval request on access grants (26.8%) are the engine-verified 80.3% vital few; the Welch t confirms access grants run ~7.4h slower than the rest even though non-access tickets alone already average 23.76h against the promise.
Assign-on-arrival dispatch rule ranked first ($0, attacks the #1 cause); pre-approved access matrix queued second; the fourth-tech hire ranked last -- capacity was never the verified cause.

After window (n=124): mean 7.22h, threshold met (vs 12.0), weakened by the declared fall-onboarding confound (direction: could only mask the win). Goal gap recovered ~104.2%. Capability at the moment of best news: stable, Cpk 0.12 -- the mean promise is kept, ~35.5% of tickets still ran over the 8-hour line.

I-MR chart frozen on the after window (center 7.22, limits 0.61/13.83); control plan monitors C1 weekly, the reopen guardrail, and dispatch-within-the-hour compliance itself; Naomi Castillo accepted the owner role 2026-10-12.

The dead end worth naming: tech capacity was investigated and ruled out early (hands-on work is only 1.9h of 26.7h) -- resisting the instinct to just hire is what let the $0 dispatch-rule fix do the work.

questions.text: Is the problem stated in measurable terms, with no cause and no fix implied?
Does the charter name a process owner who has actually agreed to the scope?
Is the business impact stated in dollars or hours, and does it hold up against an independent number?
Is the baseline built on a process the data shows is stable, not just assumed to be?
Has the measurement system itself been checked, and did it pass?
Is the operational definition tight enough that two different people would measure the same thing the same way?
Does every candidate cause carry actual evidence, not just an opinion in the room?
Are the verified causes the ones the data points to, not just the easiest ones to fix?
Has every severity-9/10 failure mode been given an action, not just logged and left?
Was exactly one change piloted at a time, with a success threshold set before the data came in?
Does the before/after proof account honestly for anything else that changed during the pilot?
How much of the original gap does this fix close, and what is the plan for what's left?
Does every monitored item have a real, named owner who has accepted the role?
Is there an out-of-control response path a person could actually follow, today, without asking what it means?
Is someone trained on the new method, by name, with a way to verify they can actually do it?
Does the realized benefit trace to the measured improvement, not to the original COPQ hope?
Are the lessons learned substantive, including at least one thing that didn't work?
Is every open item handed off to a named owner, not left to fall through?
